body.text: India is strengthening its ties with the Gulf countries even as the region is becoming more unpredictable. The visit of Indian ministers to the September 25 India-Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Troika Ministerial Meeting in New York is a reflection of how much the relations have advanced beyond the traditional markers of energy (hydrocarbon), remittances, and labour. Trade, investment, fertilizers, food security, technology, transportation, and maritime cooperation now sit alongside energy and political cooperation.

While this expansion yields economic benefits, it may also result in new sources of risks. These sectors do not operate independently: Gulf oil provides energy for Indian business and transportation; fertilizers affect agricultural production; shipping links these imports with Indian markets; Gulf investment supports infrastructure and companies; and trade relies on the same maritime routes that carry oil and other goods. Disruption of one of these links may affect others as well.

India-GCC trade in 2025–26 stood at $178.66 billion. The extent of the relationship makes this a strategic concern for both. The review of the 2024–28 Joint Action Plan during the September meeting and the commencement of negotiations on the India-GCC Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is part of the process of institutionalising the relationship. The main challenge, then, is to not diminish India’s involvement in the Gulf but stop a deepening interdependence from resulting in vulnerability.

There is a network effect in this connection. More cooperation in one area can enhance the value of another. This is because the growth in trade also necessitates more shipping; the increase in investments ensures that connectivity is reliable; industrial cooperation implies the necessity of energy and logistics; and food safety cooperation is based on agricultural production and transportation. The trade volume of $178.66 billion is, thus, not only a measure of commercial success but also indicates the scale of the economy that will be affected if the connection with the Gulf is disrupted.

It is becoming clear that the next phase of cooperation between India and the GCC will go beyond hydrocarbons. Investments from the Gulf can help build various sectors such as infrastructure, manufacturing, logistics, and technology. At the same time, Indian firms can establish a foothold in the Gulf and expand their operations throughout West Asia using Gulf logistics. The development of various projects, such as Bharat Mart in Dubai, reflects this ambition. The Ministry of Commerce has especially given priority to areas such as machinery, electronics, medical devices, drugs, processed food, and apparel.

The India-GCC FTA might serve to further consolidate this trend by introducing greater stability in the trade and investment environment. However, its value should not be judged simply on the extent to which it may increase trade volumes. Its more significant contribution would be to the possible transformation in the nature of the trade.

A relationship dominated by a limited number of strategic commodities creates one kind of vulnerability. A more diversified relationship creates more economic opportunities but it also creates more points of exposure if transport, finance, or supply chains are disrupted. Diversification, therefore, reduces sectoral concentration without eliminating geopolitical risk.

In this respect, maritime security plays a crucial role in economic policies of countries. India’s trade with the Gulf mainly relies on maritime transport, including shipping, ports, insurance, transportation fuel, and accessibility of the international waterways. The same sea routes are responsible for the delivery of energy and other vital imports, making their disruption a serious economic issue. According to the International Energy Agency, about 80 per cent of oil and oil products that pass the Strait of Hormuz are transported to Asia, with India being one of the biggest importers. Thus, problems with the route can significantly increase overall expenses for India, including energy, freight, insurance, and logistics costs.

The September meeting’s attention to commercial shipping and international waterways is significant in this context. India also acknowledged the GCC’s support in maintaining energy and fertilizer supplies despite disruptions in trade routes. This creates a fertile environment for maritime cooperation, but naval cooperation alone is not enough. Being resilient also means having alternative suppliers, diversification in shipping contracts, emergency supplies, the capacity for insurance, and logistics systems capable of absorbing disruptions.

The development of this economic relationship compliments the changes in the security environment within the Gulf. For instance, the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan demonstrates that new security ties have been established in the face of uncertainties.

But India must not overestimate the importance of the deal. It does not mean that Saudi Arabia has abandoned its relationship with India. Its wider importance is in the fact that India’s partners in the Gulf are diversifying their strategic choices. For India, this enhances the importance of good bilateral relations with the GCC countries without too much emphasis on one regional security arrangement alone. Economic interdependence cannot be completely insulated from geo-security developments.

Although diversification is a desirable goal, there are limits to it. India will not be able to quickly do away with its reliance on imported hydrocarbons. Other suppliers can be much more costly and can have much longer transport routes. Setting up other logistics networks also takes time and money. Further, an FTA cannot shield commercial relations from conflicts, sanctions, attacks on ships, and undesirable changes in policies. It has to be noted that the six GCC countries may have different priorities. The aim must be to make sure that possible disruptions in India’s relations with one of them does not lead to a destabilisation of relations with the others.

To achieve these goals, diversification has to be pursued along three lines. First, India needs to lower its high dependence on crucial imports such as crude oil, liquefied natural gas, fertilizers, and fertilizer feedstock without thinking that supplies from the Gulf can be easily replaced. India’s procurement of crude oil from Russia, Africa, and Latin America in addition to the Gulf countries is illustrative of this strategy. The procurement of fertilizers also needs to be diversified because a disruption in one source or route may adversely impact agricultural production and food security.

Second, India must consider diversifying its sectoral activities among its other partners in the Gulf as there is already a wide-ranging cooperation with the UAE in port, logistics, infrastructure, production, food corridors, and IT sectors, and initiatives like Bharat Mart aim at reaching markets beyond the Gulf. The India-GCC FTA and Joint Action Plan can establish this wider economic partnership.

Finally, redundancy in transport routes and logistics is a necessity. Some transport flows can be served using options such as Chabahar and the International North-South Transport Corridor, while the Fujairah corridor provides a partial bypass to the Strait of Hormuz. These alternatives cannot replace Gulf routes at scale, but they can provide additional options when established routes face disruption.

Thus, the deepening India-Gulf relationship represents an economic opportunity but, at the same time, serves as a test of economic resilience. The increase in value it brings cannot be separated from the increase in exposure to risk for India. The strategic task is sharper than that of merely “deepening ties”; India must develop Gulf relations while minimising the number of potential ways in which a Gulf crisis can turn into an Indian economic crisis.

Janvi Singhi is a Research Associate of Asia-Pacific Bureau at the Organization for Threat Assessment and Peacebuilding (OTAP). Era Sakhuja is Voluntary Deputy Programme Director of Emerging Technologies and Risk (ETRP) at the Centre for International Security and Economic Strategy (CISES).
The views expressed above are the authors’ own.
